newsitem.title: GERMANY: Adidas set to replace Karstadt in DAX.
newsitem.headline: Adidas set to replace Karstadt in DAX.

text.p: Adidas AG, the German sportswear group that fought off extinction at the start of the 1990s, appears set to hurdle into the prestigious DAX index and oust beleaguered retailer Karstadt AG.

Adidas is considered the top candidate to join the 30-share index on Tuesday when German stock exchange operator Deutsche Boerse and a group of German banks meet in Frankfurt for the annual review of the DAX portfolio.
Any changes to the DAX composition are expected to be announced on Tuesday afternoon. They take effect in September.

"Logic speaks for such a move but you never know what will happen," said Michael Wand, a retailing industry analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London, who gave Adidas an 85 percent chance of making it into the blue-chip index.
Adidas has declined comment on the process, which can sometimes be a political decision as banks on the panel push their favourite candidates, even ones in which they own shares.
Inclusion in the DAX index tends to stimulate demand for the stock as institutional investors reshuffle their portfolios to reflect the overall index.

Adidas' entry into the DAX would be another victory for Robert-Louis Dreyfus, who led a group of international investors that bought Adidas in early 1993 and restructured the group before the initial public offering in November 1995.
The sportswear group has shifted production to lower-cost countries in Asia and overhauled product lines to revive the heritage of Adidas' famous three-striped logo.
The group reported its best-ever results in 1996 when sales rose 35 percent to 4.7 billion marks and pre-tax profit rose 50 percent to 444 million marks.
One factor that could keep out Adidas, founded in 1920 by Adi Dassler in the Bavarian town of Herzogenaurach, would be its relatively short history as a publicly traded company.

But the top criteria support Adidas joining the DAX, as a key requirement is the so-called 35-35 rule, which says a DAX member must be among the top 35 in Germany in terms of both sales and capitalisation, according to industry analysts.
Recent German stock exchange data show Adidas occupying 27th position among German companies in terms of market capitalisation and 29th place in terms of sales.
Karstadt, on the other hand, held the 34th place in sales and was 44th in capitalisation.

Another factor favouring a switch is that Karstadt would be replaced by another consumer share in Adidas. Being in the consumer sector may have helped Karstadt stay in the DAX during the last two years.

The head of Karstadt said on Sunday in an interview that removal from the DAX could have a negative impact on Karstadt shares. But he said it did not reflect on the state of the Essen-based retailer, which has been buffeted by takeover talk.

"We would naturally regret it if we were taken out of the DAX," Karstadt chief executive Walter Deuss told "Focus" magazine. "Since the index has a meaning for institutional investors, it could have a negative impact on our shares."

Karstadt, which would be relegated to the MDAX index of medium-sized companies if replaced by Adidas in the DAX, has been dogged by low trading volumes and doubts about Deuss's ability to turn around a group with persistent problems.
Dealers, however, say Adidas shares have priced in a move into the DAX index, having nearly doubled to 220 marks now from 130 at the start of the year.
In last year's DAX review, tyremaker Continental AG was ousted to admit Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG, the giant reinsurer which had long lobbied for a position in the index.
The exchange also announced plans to remove metals group Metallgesellschaft AG to make room for the giant Deutsche Telekom AG flotation in November.
